# **Belva Davis: A Life in the Light — The Story Arc of a Trailblazer**

## 🌱 **Beginning: Roots in Resilience (Early Life & Education)**  
*“I learned to survive. And, as I moved from place to place, I learned to adapt.”*

Born Belvagene Melton on October 13, 1932, in Monroe, Louisiana, Belva was the oldest of four children. Her mother was just 14 when she gave birth — a fact that shaped Belva’s early understanding of hardship and resilience. Raised in a household of instability, she spent her formative years living with relatives across Louisiana and California.  

At age eight, her family moved to a crowded two-bedroom apartment in West Oakland, California — home to eleven people. In this tight-knit, resource-scarce environment, Belva learned survival, adaptability, and the quiet strength of perseverance.  

She excelled academically, becoming the first in her family to graduate from high school — earning her diploma from Berkeley High in 1951. Though she was accepted into San Francisco State University, financial barriers kept her from attending college. Instead, she worked as a typist at the Oakland Naval Supply Depot, earning $2,000 a year — a modest beginning, but a foundation of discipline and work ethic.

## ⚔️ **Struggle: Breaking Barriers in a Racially Hostile World**  
*“We were chased out of the Cow Palace by convention attendees throwing food at us.”*

Belva’s path to journalism was paved with obstacles — both financial and racial.  

In 1957, she began writing freelance articles for *Jet*, a publication focused on African-American life, earning $5 per piece with no byline. This early work gave her voice and confidence. She soon expanded her writing to the *Sun Reporter* and *Bay Area Independent*, eventually editing the *Sun Reporter* from 1961 to 1968 — a rare achievement for a Black woman at the time.

Her first on-air role came in 1961 as an interviewer on KSAN, a radio station serving Black listeners in the Bay Area. In 1963, she made her television debut covering an African-American beauty pageant on KTVU.  

But the real turning point came in 1964 — while covering the Republican National Convention at the Cow Palace in Daly City. Belva and her colleague Louis Freeman were chased from the event by angry white attendees who threw food and hurled racial slurs. That night, she realized: *journalism wasn’t just about reporting — it was about standing up, even when it was dangerous.*  

She continued to face racism throughout her career. In 1967, during a Civil Rights march in Forsyth County, Georgia, she was spat upon by a white woman while attempting to interview her. These experiences didn’t break her — they forged her resolve.

## 🌟 **Rise: Breaking Ground and Building a Legacy**  
*“She became the first female African-American television journalist on the West Coast.”*

In 1966, Belva Davis made history — becoming the **first African-American woman to report on television in the U.S. West Coast** when she was hired by KPIX-TV, the CBS affiliate in San Francisco.  

Over the next three decades, she became a trusted anchor and a respected voice on Bay Area television. She anchored news at KPIX (starting in 1970) and later moved to KRON-TV, the local NBC affiliate.  

Her reporting covered pivotal moments in American history:  
- The Berkeley Free Speech Movement riots  
- The rise of the Black Panthers  
- The Jonestown mass suicide-murder  
- The assassinations of Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk  
- The AIDS and crack epidemics  
- The 1998 U.S. embassy bombing in Tanzania  

Through it all, she maintained a calm, dignified presence — a rare quality in a field often dominated by tension and emotion. As fellow reporter Rita Williams put it: *“Belva knew instinctively how to keep everyone in check. She had so much class, so much presence, so much intuition. Belva has always been the grande dame.”*

In 1981, she co-hosted *California This Week* with Rollin Post for 18 years — a platform that brought serious, thoughtful conversation to millions of viewers.
